From Physiological Responses to Dynamic Thermal Sensation: A State-Space Modeling Framework for Inferring Latent Thermal States Abstract Thermal comfort research has largely relied on steady-state assumptions, leaving the mechanisms by which internal physiological configurations mediate thermal perception un- der dynamic conditions insufficiently understood. This study introduces a latent thermal state framework that models thermoregulation as a dynamical system linking environmen- tal forcing, physiological responses, and thermal sensation. Using multimodal wearable recordings from seven participants in naturalistic environments (the Car Office Comfort, COC dataset), we employ a state-space modelling approach that combines discrete and con- tinuous representations of latent thermal states. An Input-Output Hidden Markov Model (IO-HMM) identifies six semantically coherent thermal regimes spanning a physiological con- tinuum from cool comfort to extreme heat stress, while a Linear Dynamical System (LDS) captures three continuous latent dimensions operating at distinct timescales (τ ≈ 15.3, 9.3, and 5.8 min). Across both representations, the dominant physiological driver of thermal sensation shifts systematically along the thermal continuum, from skin temperature under cool-to-neutral conditions to electrodermal activity under moderate and extreme thermal loading. Analysis of transition dynamics further shows that physiological volatility scales with the thermal hierarchy of the states involved with a clear directional asymmetry between warming and cooling transitions. These findings provide a mechanistically interpretable perspective on thermal perception dynamics and support the development of physiologically informed, closed-loop thermal control strategies in dynamic built environments. Keywords: Dynamic thermal comfort, State-space models, Hidden Markov models, Thermal comfort, Physiological signals 1. Introduction Thermal comfort research has long focused on steady-state conditions, in which the thermal environment and the human body are assumed to be in equilibrium and physiological responses have fully stabilised. The Predicted Mean Vote (PMV) model developed by Fanger [1] embodies this paradigm by estimating thermal sensation from a set of environmental and personal parameters under thermally stable conditions. The model remains a cornerstone of built environment evaluation and is embedded in major standards, including ASHRAE Standard 55 [2] and ISO 7730 [3]. Although adaptive comfort models [4, 5] later extended this framework to account for climatic and behavioural adaptation, most existing approaches continue to infer comfort from static environment snapshots, with limited consideration of the temporal dynamics of human thermoregulation. In practice, occupants frequently encounter dynamic thermal conditions—transitions be- tween indoor and outdoor spaces, in-vehicle commuting, or buildings with fluctuating cooling and heating operation. Under these conditions, thermal perception emerges from a tempo- rally evolving interaction between environmental stimuli and physiological regulation rather than from a single environmental state. Laboratory studies have characterised transient thermal responses under controlled perturbations such as step changes and ramped expo- sures [6, 7, 8]; while these studies provide important insights into transient sensation, they primarily characterise responses to experimentally imposed stimuli in controlled settings, leaving open the question of how thermal perception unfolds in naturally varying environ- ments. Recent advances in wearable sensing have opened a path to studying this question in the field: physiological signals such as heart rate (HR), skin temperature (Tskin ), and elec- trodermal activity (EDA), which reflect thermoregulatory load and autonomic activation, have been increasingly explored as real-world comfort indicators [9]. However, the majority of the existing data-driven, especially machine learning models treat these signals as discrim- inative predictors of reported sensation, without representing the underlying physiological mechanisms that generate them [10, 11, 12, 13], leaving the intermediate processes linking thermoregulatory response to subjective perception underexplored. This mechanistic gap is not merely a modelling choice but has theoretical grounding. Thermoregulation operates as a state-dependent dynamical system [14, 15, 16], and the theory of alliesthesia [17] demonstrates that the hedonic evaluation of thermal stimuli de- pends on the body’s internal state rather than on stimulus magnitude alone. Together, these perspectives suggest that comfort perception is mediated by an internal physiological configuration that evolves continuously over time; yet this latent thermal state has rarely been operationalised as an explicit construct in empirical research. This study addresses this gap by modelling thermal perception as a dynamical system in which a latent thermal state is inferred from continuous multimodal physiological obser- vations under naturally varying conditions. We employ a state-space modelling framework combining an Input-Output Hidden Markov Model (IO-HMM) for discrete regime identi- fication and a Linear Dynamical System (LDS) for continuous latent dynamics, applied to physiological recordings from an naturalistic dataset. The analysis investigates whether stable, interpretable latent states can be recovered from physiological data, how state transi- tions align with subjective thermal sensation, and whether transient physiological responses constitute a distinct mode of thermal state activity characterised by abrupt transitions and elevated thermoregulatory load. 2. Background and Literature Review 2.1. Dynamic thermal comfort A substantial body of laboratory research has characterised transient thermal responses under controlled perturbations. Typical experimental protocols include step changes be- tween two fixed ambient temperatures, continuous ramps or drifts, and cyclic thermal vari- 2 ations [6, 18]. The classic step-change studies of Gagge et al. [19], conducted using twin climate chambers in which subjects moved between rooms of differing temperatures after a stabilisation period, showed that thermal sensation lead rather than follow body tempera- ture changes, which is an anticipatory effect that was most pronounced under cold exposures. De Dear et al. [20] extended this line of work and documented an overshoot phenomenon: the initial sensation magnitude following a downward temperature step was approximately twice that of the equivalent upward step, revealing a fundamental directional asymmetry in the human thermal perceptual system. Beyond environmental manipulations, Jia et al. [21] investigated transitions between activity states and found that subjective thermal re- sponses are similarly governed by core temperature receptor dynamics and exhibit the same cold-greater-than-warm asymmetry. Taken together, these findings establish that thermal sensation depends not only on the magnitude of the thermal load but also on its direction and rate of change, reflecting a temporally structured, nonlinear perceptual system. These laboratory investigations provide essential empirical foundations; by design, how- ever, they characterise responses to experimentally imposed perturbations in carefully con- trolled settings. How thermal perception evolves under the naturally varying, multi-source thermal exposures encountered in real environments, where transitions are irregular, dura- tions are unconstrained, and no single stimulus is cleanly isolated, has received comparatively limited empirical attention. 2.2. The thermal state: an internal physiological mediator The proposal that thermal perception depends on an internal physiological state rather than on stimulus properties alone has a long theoretical lineage. Cabanac [17] introduced the concept of alliesthesia to describe how the hedonic valence of a sensory stimulus, which denote its perceived pleasantness or unpleasantness, is determined by the body’s momentary internal state: cooling the skin is pleasant when the body is overheated but unpleasant when it is already cold, irrespective of the absolute temperature applied. De Dear [22] revisited this hypothesis in the context of the built environment, arguing that the pleasure or displeasure of a thermal sensation is not bound to stimulus magnitude but is mediated by internal signals reflecting deviation from physiological set points. Neurophysiological evidence reviewed by Vellei et al. [18] further grounds this framing: the perception of innocuous skin warming depends on the inhibition of cold-activated neurons, indicating that the thermal sensation system encodes a complex, state-dependent function of the thermal load trajectory rather than its instantaneous value. The term thermal state has appeared in various forms in the built-environment literature, though rarely as a formally operationalised construct. Data-driven attempts to partially capture thermal dynamics have been made. The Personalised Dynamic Thermal Comfort (PDTC) model [23], for instance, incorporates temporal structure through autoregressive components and individual-specific coefficients grounded in heat-balance principles. How- ever, such models largely rely on aggregated occupant feedback as their primary learning signal and do not directly infer the internal physiological configuration that mediates be- tween environmental exposure and perceived sensation. This gap motivates an approach that treats the thermal state as a latent variable to be inferred from continuous multimodal 3 physiological observations within an explicit dynamical model, which is a perspective that state-space modelling frameworks are particularly well suited to provide. 2.3. State-space modeling in built environment and thermal comfort studies State-space models (SSMs), as a classical framework in control theory and signal pro- cessing [24], have a well-established presence in building and indoor environment research. Early Markovian formulations treated thermal and occupancy conditions as discrete ob- servable states with stochastic transition dynamics, serving primarily as tools for building energy simulation [25, 26]. More recent work has extended this framework to recover la- tent behavioural profiles from smart meter data [27], to estimate discrete occupant activity states from building sensor streams [28], and to predict indoor temperature conditioned on hidden occupant preference states via IO-HMM [29]. Physics-informed state-space represen- tations have also been derived from building thermal circuits to support model-based control [30]. Taken together, these studies demonstrate the utility of latent-state representations for characterising building thermal dynamics, although their primary focus has remained on system-level energy and physical quantities rather than on the perceptual experience of occupants. A smaller body of work has explored probabilistic state representations in closer relation to thermal perception. [31] formulated thermal sensation dynamics as a linear state-space system driven by indoor environmental inputs, enabling real-time comfort estimation for closed-loop building control. [32] employed an unsupervised HMM to identify discrete ther- mal comfort states from infrared thermography without requiring subjective comfort votes, demonstrating that latent comfort regimes can be inferred from observational data alone. These studies offer valuable demonstrations of a latent-state perspective on comfort; in both cases, however, the inferred states are grounded in environmental measurements or passive surface temperatures rather than in the multimodal physiological signals that more directly reflect thermoregulatory activation and autonomic load. In parallel, the proliferation of wearable sensing platforms has expanded the observa- tional basis for comfort modelling. A substantial body of work has demonstrated that Tskin , HR (and its variability), and EDA carry information predictive of thermal sensation and can be used to classify comfort states across a variety of indoor environments, with both conventional machine learning and deep learning approaches achieving strong predictive performance [9, 10, 33, 34, 35]. However, these models are primarily optimised to map phys- iological observations to sensation labels; the internal thermoregulatory state that mediates between environmental exposure and perceived sensation is not explicitly represented and remains implicit in the learned mapping. Taken together, the foregoing review points to three inter-related gaps. First, empirical evidence on dynamic thermal perception remains concentrated in laboratory perturbation paradigms; how comfort states evolve under ecologically valid, naturally varying thermal exposures has been comparatively less studied. Second, while physiological signals have been shown to be informative predictors of sensation, existing models treat them as dis- criminative inputs without explicitly representing the intermediate thermoregulatory state that links environmental exposure to perception. Third, although state-space models have 4 been applied to building energy systems and to limited comfort-state inference tasks, they have not been extended to recovering a continuously evolving latent thermal state from multimodal physiological data under real-world conditions. 3. Methodology 3.1. Overview This study proposes an integrated state-space modelling (SSM) framework to uncover latent thermal states from continuous physiological signals and examine how these states relate to thermal sensation under dynamical real-world environmental conditions (Figure 1). Physiological and environmental signals from the Car Office Comfort (COC) dataset [36] are first consolidated into structured session-based sequences, which are modelled using state- space approaches to extract both discrete regimes and continuous latent dynamics. The framework examines how physiological dynamics govern transitions between latent ther- mal states and evaluates how both steady and transient state patterns align with thermal sensations. Figure 1: Overview of the analytical framework. Left: physiological and environmental inputs from the COC dataset. Centre: latent thermal state modelling via IO-HMM (discrete regimes) and LDS (continuous latent dynamics), with a derived Transient Index (TI). Right: thermal sensation representation based on adaptive comfort and transfer-learned TSV labels. 3.2. Dataset 3.2.1. Car Office Comfort (COC) dataset As the primary dataset, the COC dataset [36] contains multimodal physiological and environmental recordings from eight subjects (S01–S08) during their daily commuting and office routines in Perugia, Italy, across the summer of 2023. Physiological signals, including electrodermal activity (EDA, 4 Hz), heart rate (HR, 1 Hz), and peripheral skin temperature (Tskin , 4 Hz), were continuously recorded using the Empatica E4 wristband. Environmental 5 conditions were captured by Button thermohygrometers (air temperature Ta and relative humidity RH, ∼min resolution) deployed in four nodes across the car interior and at each participant’s office desk, supplemented by a wireless sensor network monitoring office-level illuminance, door/window states, and air temperature at 5-min intervals. Because the study was designed to follow participants’ undisturbed daily routines, no self-reported thermal sensation votes (TSV) were collected. 3.2.2. Thermal supervision dataset (TSD) To provide supervisory signals for thermal sensation, we collected a secondary thermal supervision dataset (TSD) to supply supervisory signals for TSV estimation. The exper- iment was conducted in student dormitories at Chongqing University during July–August 2024. Thirty-two healthy university students (14 male, 18 female; age 21±1 years) who had resided in the local climate for over two years participated under sedentary conditions with standardized light clothing (∼0.5 clo). Each 3-hour session was sampled at 10-minute intervals, yielding 1,035 records in total. At each sampling point, participants reported their thermal sensation on the ASHRAE 7-point scale (TSV ∈ −3, . . . , +3) [2]. Concurrent physiological and environmental measurements were recorded, including skin temperature (Tskin ; infrared thermometer, ±0.2,◦ C), heart rate (HR; Huawei Band 9, ±10 bpm), indoor air temperature (Ta ) and relative humidity (RH), both measured using a HOBO UX100-011 temperature-humidity data logger (accuracy: ±0.21,◦ C for temperature and ±2.5% for RH; observed ranges 24.1-33.0 °C and 20.8-73.8%, respectively). Obvious physiological outliers were removed prior to analysis. 3.2.3. Integrated Surface Database (ISD) To calculate the running mean outdoor temperature (RMOT) required by adaptive com- fort, hourly surface meteorological observations were obtained from the NOAA Integrated Surface Database (ISD) [37]. Candidate stations within 50 km of each study site (Perugia, Italy and Chongqing, China) were identified and dataset with higher data coverage for the study time period is selected. All recorded observations contained valid Ta readings, with hourly coverage of 99.2% for Perugia (17,265 records, sub-hourly frequency) and 95.7% for Chongqing (8,408 obs, hourly frequency), which are resampled to daily-mean for RMOT calculation. 3.3. Data preprocessing and representation 3.3.1. Data consolidation The raw multi-rate physiological and environmental recordings from COC dataset were aligned and merged per subject. Continuous recordings were first segmented into contiguous sessions by identifying temporal gaps exceeding 30 minutes, yielding a set of segments per subject. Within each segment, all physiological and environmental channels were jointly resampled to a uniform 10-second resolution via mean aggregation. Across all eight subjects, this produced 289 labeled sessions totaling approximately 120.5 hours of synchronized data (see Appendix Table A.2 for per-subject details). 6 All subsequent filtering and consolidation steps were guided by two principles: (i) preserv- ing mechanistic consistency of physiological responses, and (ii) ensuring temporal stability for reliable state modelling. Accordingly, modelling was restricted to the in-car environ- ment, where physiological responses are more directly coupled to thermal exposure. Office recordings were excluded due to their greater susceptibility to non-thermal stressors (e.g., cognitive workload) and their comparatively limited data volume (25.7% of total recording time), which would introduce confounding variability and reduce statistical robustness. To further enhance model stability, in-car sessions with session-averaged air temperature ex- ceeding 40 °C were removed (6.6% of total in-car recording time), as these rare extreme exposures are sparsely represented in the supervisory dataset and may exert disproportion- ate leverage during parameter estimation. Subject S04 was additionally excluded due to limited datasize and excessive temporal fragmentation (4.8 total hours across 22 short ses- sions), which precluded reliable dynamic modelling. The final dataset used for modelling and analysis comprises seven subjects and 129 in-car sessions with 426,713 records in total. 3.3.2. Thermal sensation representation Given the absence of self-reported TSV in COC dataset, we represent thermal sensation using two complementary indicators. The first is the Adaptive Comfort Deviation (ACD), a physically grounded measure that quantifies the deviation of the indoor operative temper- ature from the adaptive neutral temperature predicted based on the ASHRAE 55 adaptive comfort model [2]. Although the adaptive model was originally formulated for naturally ventilated buildings, it is employed here not as a strict comfort compliance criterion but as a climate-adjusted reference for neutral thermal expectation. The derived ACD therefore provides an external independent benchmark describing the thermodynamic departure of the observed environment from a climate-adapted neutral point. The second is a transferred pseudo-TSV label obtained via ordinal regression trained on TSD. It serves as a perception-oriented extrapolation across domains, enabling physiological observations in COC to be interpreted on the subjective thermal sensation scale. Together, these two indicators provide complementary lenses on thermal sensation and enable a form of cross-validation. ACD offers an independent comfort-theoretic reference derived from established field evidence, whereas pseudo-TSV contributes a data-driven approximation of subjective perception grounded in labelled observations. Adaptive comfort deviation (ACD). ACD is defined as the signed deviation from the adaptive neutral temperature Tcomf [2]. The neutral temperature is computed as Tcomf = 0.31 Trm + 17.8 (1) ∞ X Trm (d) = (1 − α) αi−1 T out (d − i), α = 0.8 (2) i=1 where Trm is the RMOT and T out is the daily mean outdoor temperature derived from local ISD records. The ASHRAE 55 acceptability bands correspond to ±3.5◦ C (80%) and ±2.5◦ C 7 (90%) around Tcomf . The ACD is then defined as δ = Top − Tcomf , (3) where Top is the indoor operative temperature, approximated as the average of air tempera- ture Ta and mean radiant temperature Tr (Tr = Ta when radiant temperature is unavailable). TSV transfer learning via ordinal regression. We train a thermal sensation model on TSD and transfer it to COC to assign pseudo-TSV labels. Two factors jointly constrain the choice of transfer model. First, the moderate scale of TSD (N = 1,035) limits the effective capacity of machine-learning methods and risks overfitting to its specific distributional characteris- tics. Second, a pronounced distribution shift between the two datasets exits. Particularly, around 20% of in-car COC records have Ta > 35 °C, which is a regime not represented in TSD. This distribution shift problem undermines the reliability of data-driven machine learning models when extrapolating to unseen thermal conditions. We therefore adopt ordi- nal logistic regression (OLR), a classic parametric model whose proportional odds structure imposes physiologically consistent monotonicity constraints and generalises more robustly under covariate shift: P (TSV ≤ j | x) = σ θj − β ⊤ x , j ∈ {−3, . . . , +2},  (4) where x = [HR, Ta , RH, PMV]⊤ is the feature vector of physiological and environmental predictors, θj is the cumulative log-odds threshold separating sensation category j from warmer categories, and β is a shared coefficient vector. The model is fitted on TSD and produces, for each COC record, a full posterior over the seven TSV levels; the point estimate used in downstream analyses is +3 X E[TSV] = k · P (TSV = k | x). (5) k=−3 Importantly, the objective of the OLR model in this context is not to produce accurate TSV predictions for the COC dataset. The transfer spans datasets collected under substan- tially different experimental conditions and behavioural context. Rather than treating the transferred TSV as reconstructions of subjective votes, we use the OLR model as a physiolog- ically interpretable mapping that places the COC observations on an approximate thermal sensation scale consistent with established thermal comfort relationships. The pseudo-TSV labels should therefore be interpreted as a structured latent indicator of thermal load, rather than as precise reconstructions of individual subjective votes. Furthermore, by using the probability-weighted expectation of TSV rather than hard class assignments, the model pre- serves uncertainty information and reduces the potential amplification of domain bias near decision boundaries. 3.3.3. Feature engineering and specifications HR decomposition. Within the consolidated dataset, HR was decomposed into two compo- nents to separate time-scales of cardiovascular response: a slow trend (HRlow ) extracted via 8 a centered 5-minute rolling mean, and a high-frequency residual (HRhigh = HR − HRlow ) capturing acute beat-to-beat fluctuations. This frequency-scale separation mitigates the sen- sitivity of discrete state modelling to high-frequency noise while preserving both sustained and phasic cardiovascular information. PMV specifications. PMV was computed as a composite thermal load predictor rather than direct thermal senstation proxy following the ASHRAE 55 standard [2], implemented using the pythermalcomfort library [38]. The mean radiant temperature was approximated by the ambient air temperature (Tr = Ta ), a common simplification for indoor environments without strong radiant asymmetry. Air velocity was fixed at v = 0.1 m/s to represent near- still indoor conditions, and input temperatures were clipped to the ASHRAE applicability range [10, 40] °C prior to computation. Clothing insulation was set to Icl = 0.5 clo, consistent with light summer clothing observed in the study protocols. Metabolic rate was set to a baseline value of M = 1.2 met (light sedentary activity) and adjusted at the individual level using subject height and weight via the Du Bois body surface area (BSA) formulation [39]. The effective metabolic rate was scaled proportionally to the ratio between the subject- specific BSA and the ISO reference body [3]. 3.4. State-space modelling of thermal regime dynamics To capture latent thermal states as a mediator between physiological responses and ther- mal sensation, we formulate thermal adaptation as a state-space process driven by physio- logical autocorrelation and environmental forcing. Let t = 1, . . . , T denote discrete time steps. At each time step, the physiological obser- vation vector is defined as yt ∈ RN , by default containing HRlow , HRhigh , Tskin , tonic and phasic electrodermal activity (EDAtonic , EDAphasic ). Environmental forcing is represented by an input vector ut ∈ RM , comprising Ta and RH. The latent variable zt represents the underlying thermoregulatory state governing the organisation of physiological responses. Conceptually, the latent thermal state zt evolves according to an input-conditioned Markov process, zt ∼ p(zt | zt−1 , ut ), via the transition distribution. Conditioned on the current latent state zt , the physiological observation yt is generated from a state-dependent emission model, yt ∼ p(yt | zt ), parameterised by an emission matrix or distribution (e.g., Gaussian emissions). Formally, the joint distribution factorises as T Y T Y p(z1:T , y1:T | u1:T ) = p(z ) p(zt | zt−1 , ut ) p(yt | zt ) . | {z1} t=2 t=1 initial distribution | {z } | {z } transition model emission model The latent thermal state zt is modelled in either discrete or continous form as elaborated in Section 3.4.1 and 3.4.2. 3.4.1. Input-Output Hidden Markov Model (IO-HMM): Identification of discrete thermal regimes An IO-HMM [40] is applied for identification of qualitatively distinct thermal regimes zt and allows environmental inputs ut to modulate transition probabilities between them. The 9 model is implemented using the ssm library [41]. Initial distribution. Let zt ∈ {1, . . . , K} denote the discrete latent thermal regime at time t. The Pinitial regime is drawn from a categorical distribution, P (z1 = k) = πk , where π ∈ RK and K k=1 πk = 1. Input-conditioned transitions. To allow environmental forcing to modulate regime switching, we adopt an input-conditioned transition model of the form P (zt | zt−1 , ut ). Specifically, given the previous regime zt−1 = j and input vector ut ∈ RM , the probability of transitioning into regime k is defined as an input-modulated mapping of a baseline transition matrix A. Specifically, P (zt = k | zt−1 = j, ut ) = softmaxk (log Aj,· + W ut ) , where A ∈ RK×K + is a row-stochastic baseline transition matrix and ut ∈ RM denotes the environmental forcing vector. The modulation function is defined via a multinomial logistic (softmax) transformation, which guarantees non-negativity and row normalisation while allowing environmental variables to bias regime-switching tendencies. Gaussian emission. Conditioned on the current discrete regime, physiological observations are modelled by a state-specific multivariate Gaussian distribution: p(yt | zt = k) = N (yt ; µk , Σk ), k = 1, . . . , K, where µk ∈ RN and Σk ∈ RN ×N denote the regime-specific mean vector and covariance matrix, respectively. This emission specification allows each thermal regime to encode a distinct multivariate physiological profile and within-regime variability. Model fitting. Model parameters Θ = {π, A, W, µk , Σk }Kk=1 are estimated by maximum likeli- hood using the standard expectation–maximization (EM) algorithm [42]. The objective is to maximize the conditional data likelihood p(y1:T | u1:T ; Θ) (equivalently, the log-likelihood). Following the implementation, IO-HMM training uses the full consolidated in-car dataset (all retained subjects/segments), with observations z-scored by a global pooled scaler before fitting a single shared model. 3.4.2. Linear Dynamical System (LDS): Continuous latent modelling of regime dynamics While the IO-HMM emphasises regime identification and interpretable switching struc- ture, it represents thermal dynamics as a finite set of discrete regimes, thereby approximating potentially continuous physiological adaptation with piecewise-constant states. The LDS is therefore leveraged to describe the continuous latent space, emphasising dynamical evolution and intrinsic adaptation timescales. Initial distribution. In the LDS formulation, the latent thermal state is continuous, zt ∈ RD . The initial state is modeled as z1 ∼ N (µ0 , P0 ), where µ0 ∈ RD and P0 ∈ RD×D denote the initial mean and covariance. 10 Input-conditioned latent dynamics. Environmental forcing enters the latent transition equa- tion linearly: zt = Azt−1 + But + qt , qt ∼ N (0, Q), where A ∈ RD×D is the latent transition matrix, B ∈ RD×M is the input loading matrix, and Q ∈ RD×D is the process-noise covariance. Gaussian observation model. Physiological observations are generated by a linear-Gaussian emission model: yt = Czt + rt , rt ∼ N (0, R), equivalently, p(yt | zt ) = N (yt ; Czt , R), where C ∈ RN ×D is the observation matrix and R ∈ RN ×N is the observation-noise covari- ance. Model fitting. Similarly, parameters Θ = {µ0 , P0 , A, B, C, Q, R} are estimated by maximum likelihood using the EM procedure for linear Gaussian state-space models [43]. In the E-step, posterior moments of the latent states are computed using the Kalman filter and Rauch- Tung-Striebel (RTS) smoother. Because reliable estimation of LDS dynamical parameters, particularly the process of the noise covariance matrices (Q and R), requires sufficiently continuous and dynamically stable trajectories, the analysis is restricted to subject S01, which provides the longest and most temporally coherent recording. The LDS is therefore employed as an in-depth single-subject case study to characterise the continuous latent dynamics of physiological responses. Dynamical timescale interpretation. The eigenvalues of the transition matrix A determine the intrinsic relaxation timescales of the latent dynamical modes. For a discrete-time system with sampling interval ∆t, each eigenvalue λi corresponds to an equivalent continuous-time decay constant [44] ∆t τi = − , ln |λi | representing the characteristic time for perturbations along the corresponding mode to decay to approximately e−1 (about 37%) of their initial magnitude. Larger τi therefore indicate slower latent adaptation processes, whereas smaller values correspond to faster physiological adjustments. In this way, the LDS decomposes the latent thermal dynamics into a small set of approximately independent dynamical modes, each associated with a distinct mean- reversion timescale. Together, the complementary formulations IO-HMM and LDS provide a structured rep- resentation of latent thermal regime dynamics, capturing both discrete regime transitions and continuous adaptation processes within a unified state-space framework. 11 3.5. Transient dynamics of regime transitions Latent state representations describe the structural organisation of thermoregulatory dy- namics, whether expressed as discrete regimes or as coordinates in a continuous latent space. However, the latent state at a given time primarily indicates where the physiological system resides, rather than how dynamically perturbed it is. In particular, neither regime identity nor latent position directly reflects whether the system is in a stable steady configuration or undergoing rapid adjustment to a changing thermal load. To examine these within- and peri-transition dynamics, we construct a continuous Tran- sient Index (TI) that quantifies moment-to-moment physiological volatility, and use it to characterise the temporal structure of physiological responses around regime transition events. 3.5.1. Construction of the physiological transient index For each time step t within the sessions, we compute two rolling statistics over a centred 2-minute window: the rolling standard deviation and the rolling temporal slope (first order difference) of each physiological signal, i.e., HR, Tskin , EDAphasic , and EDAtonic . The stan- dard deviation quantifies local fluctuation magnitude, while the slope captures the rate and direction of ongoing change. Together, these rolling features form a feature vector ϕt ∈ RF describing the local volatility profile at each time step. Because the individual rolling features operate on different physiological channels with different scales and are partly correlated, we reduce them to a single scalar index via principal component analysis (PCA).
